edges.effect_quant: Meta-analyses of observational Barrett surveillance studies suggest lower esophageal-adenocarcinoma mortality among regularly surveilled patients and among surveillance-detected cancers, but the most rigorous community-based case-control study did not confirm a substantial mortality reduction, leaving the net effect unsettled.
edges.population: patients with Barrett esophagus undergoing periodic endoscopic surveillance for dysplasia or early esophageal adenocarcinoma
edges.mechanism: Surveillance can find dysplasia or intramucosal adenocarcinoma earlier, allowing endoscopic eradication therapy or surgery at a more treatable stage before metastatic progression.
edges.summary: This is a genuinely contested surveillance edge. Observational meta-analyses generally point toward lower mortality and earlier-stage detection, yet the best case-control evaluation found no clear reduction in adenocarcinoma death, so a mixed direction is more honest than a uniformly protective label.
edges.caveats: Lead-time bias, length bias, and selection of healthier patients into surveillance programs remain major interpretation problems. Much of the literature compares surveillance-detected with symptom-detected cancer, which can exaggerate apparent benefit if not carefully adjusted.

evidence.notes: The Effect of Endoscopic Surveillance in Patients With Barrett's Esophagus: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.

effect_quant.comparator: EAC-related and all-cause mortality among regularly surveilled Barrett esophagus patients versus those not regularly surveilled across cohort studies

evidence.citation: Qiao Y et al 2015 Clin Transl Gastroenterol
evidence.notes: Surveillance in Patients With Barrett's Esophagus for Early Detection of Esophageal Adenocarcinoma: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

effect_quant.comparator: mortality among surveillance-detected esophageal adenocarcinoma versus nonsurveillance-detected esophageal adenocarcinoma
